title: SYSK Selects: How Fossils Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the episode "How Fossils Work," chosen by Josh as a favorite that still holds up. The hosts explain what a fossil is (preserved remains or traces of once-living material that have undergone fossilization, mostly found in sedimentary rock in the Earth's crust). They cover trace fossils (footprints, tracks/trackways, tooth marks, coprolites or fossilized dung), body fossils like bones, and the process by which sediment buries remains, organic material decays, and minerals such as calcium, iron and carbonate replace or fortify the bone. Other preservation routes discussed include petrified wood, desiccation in dry caves, freezing (Liuba the baby woolly mammoth), tar pits (La Brea), peat bogs (Tollund Man), and amber (the Jurassic Park DNA idea, which the hosts say is debunked). The episode covers how fossils are dated (carbon-14 limited to about 60,000 years, potassium-40 and uranium-238 for millions of years), how to excavate them carefully with plaster jackets and a plane of weakness, the fossil record's incompleteness, transitional fossils such as the baleen whale ancestor, punctuated equilibrium versus gradual evolution (Stephen J. Gould), and living fossils like the horseshoe crab, ginkgo and coelacanth. Also covers Lucy's newly found foot bones showing upright walking. The episode ends with listener mail about a young marimba player who was upset about a bronze medal.

segments.title: Opening banter and Lucy's foot bones
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode and the hosts discuss the article's comprehensiveness, then Lucy the 3.2 million-year-old hominid, whose newly found foot bones showed she walked upright.

segments.title: Types of fossils: trace versus body fossils
segments.summary: The hosts describe trace fossils such as footprints, trackways and tooth marks, and body fossils like bones, and define a fossil as once-living material that has undergone fossilization.

segments.title: Sedimentary rock and how bones fossilize
segments.summary: Most fossils are found in sedimentary rock in the crust. Burial by sediment protects remains from decomposition, organic material breaks down, and minerals such as calcium, iron and carbonate fill the pores of the bone, turning it into rock in the bone's shape.

segments.title: Molds, casts, and dung fossils
segments.summary: Trace fossils can form as molds or casts of footprints filled by sediment, and fossilized feces (coprolites) can reveal diet. Josh and Chuck joke about a CIA attempt to analyze Gorbachev's stool.

segments.title: Other preservation: desiccation, freezing, tar, peat, amber
segments.summary: Petrified wood is discussed, then desiccation in dry caves preserving skin, freezing preserving baby woolly mammoth Liuba, La Brea tar pits, Tollund Man in peat bog, and amber, including the Jurassic Park DNA idea that the hosts say was debunked.

segments.title: Why fossils are rare and where to find them
segments.summary: Only a tiny fraction of organisms become fossils, and fossils must be found in rock of the right age. Radiocarbon dating only reaches about 60,000 years, so isotopes such as potassium-40 and uranium-238 are used for older rock.

segments.title: Excavating and dating fossils
segments.summary: Advice on digging up fossils: call a museum, use cranes and plaster jackets for slabs, flake rock along the plane of weakness, reinforce brittle bone with resin and glue, and keep context. The hosts note CT scanning is used for study rather than dating.

segments.title: Fossil record, transitional fossils, and punctuated equilibrium
segments.summary: The fossil record is incomplete, and transitional fossils such as the baleen whale with teeth help show evolution. Stephen J. Gould's punctuated equilibrium proposes evolution in fast bursts, which explains gaps. Living fossils like the horseshoe crab, ginkgo and coelacanth are covered.

segments.title: Listener mail: the marimba bronze medal
segments.summary: A listener named Ali, a marimba player from Indiana, wrote that she was upset after earning a bronze medal at a state band contest. The hosts respond sympathetically and the segment closes with the call for listener mail.
